one_liner: Pure-Go TOML 1.1 library with an encoding/json-style API; project benchmarks show 2.4-6.4x faster than BurntSushi/toml.
what_it_does: Decodes TOML 1.1 into Go structs, maps and interface{} values, and encodes them back. The API follows encoding/json: toml.Unmarshal/Marshal, NewDecoder(r).Decode(v), NewEncoder(w).Encode(v), `toml:"name,omitempty,inline,multiline,commented"` struct tags, TextMarshaler/TextUnmarshaler support, and a strict mode (DisallowUnknownFields) that reports keys with no matching field. Extras: LocalDate/LocalTime/LocalDateTime types, DecodeError messages that point at the failing line and column, output with comments, and an `unstable` package with an AST-level Parser, Marshaler/Unmarshaler interfaces, RawMessage, and a comment-preserving document editor (unstable/edit, which is on the v2 branch but not yet in a tagged release).
how_it_is_fast: A from-scratch rewrite of the parser, decoder and encoder (PR #1067, June 2026) stores AST nodes in one reusable flat arena ([]Node with int32 handles). It scans comments and strings 8 bytes at a time with SWAR bit tricks (hasByteBelow/hasByteEqual on uint64 words), validates UTF-8 one run at a time, and returns strings without escapes as zero-copy subslices of the input. The decoder state (arena, duplicate-key tracker, scratch buffers) is reused through sync.Pool; key strings are interned; struct field lookups use a per-type plan cached in a sync.Map with a case-folded index; and each table header is resolved once, instead of re-walking from the root for every key. interface{}/map[string]interface{} targets use a fused single-pass scanner that builds Go maps directly, with no AST nodes for scalars, and the encoder caches per-type plans and pools its buffers (Marshal/ReferenceFile/struct went from 226 to 4 allocs/op).
when_to_use: Go services and CLIs that load TOML config into structs where decode latency or allocations matter, e.g. Hugo-style batches of many small front-matter documents (Unmarshal/HugoFrontMatter: 5.9x vs BurntSushi in the README).
Decoding arbitrary TOML into map[string]interface{} or interface{} (Viper-style). This takes the fused no-reflection path, where the README's dataset benchmarks show 4.5-8.3x vs BurntSushi.
Catching config typos with DisallowUnknownFields, and giving users line/column errors (DecodeError) without writing your own.
Generating commented config templates (the `comment` tag and the `commented` option), or editing TOML in place while keeping comments (unstable/edit, not yet released).
Projects that want a stdlib-only dependency: go.mod has no requirements, the rewrite claims zero `unsafe`, and CI checks that the capslock capability baseline does not grow.
when_not_to_use: Code that relies on BurntSushi's MetaData (IsDefined, Undecoded, Keys, Type) or on Primitive/PrimitiveDecode for delayed decoding. go-toml v2's Decode returns only an error, and its RawMessage equivalent lives in the semver-exempt unstable package.

Named scalar types that implement encoding.TextUnmarshaler (e.g. `type Secret string`) on v2.4.0-v2.4.3: UnmarshalText is skipped silently (#1109). The fix (#1113), together with a MarshalText fix for named string types (#1114), is on the v2 branch but not in any tagged release as of 2026-09-25.

Untrusted input on v2.4.2 or earlier: deeply nested arrays or inline tables crash the whole process with an unrecoverable stack overflow (GHSA-frc4-6h9q-39fq, high). v2.4.3 fixes this with a nesting cap of 10000.
Very large or streamed inputs: Decoder.Decode reads the whole io.Reader into memory (io.ReadAll) before parsing, and there is no incremental decoding into values.

Risk-averse upgrades: v2.4.0 contains the June 2026 rewrite, and at least three regressions followed (#1075 broken encoder output, #1078 inline embedded structs not decoded, #1109). v2.3.x keeps the older implementation, which the pre-rewrite README measured at 2.0-5.0x vs BurntSushi on the common cases.

integration.dependencies: none (go.mod declares no requirements; stdlib only)
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod: go 1.21.0; README supports the last two major Go releases; CI tests Go 1.25 and 1.26 (the rewrite PR also reports passing on go1.22)
integration.platforms: any Go target: pure Go, no cgo, no unsafe; the word-at-a-time scanning uses portable binary.LittleEndian loads; CI runs on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS runners
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Package-level Unmarshal/Marshal take per-call state from sync.Pool and cache type plans in sync.Map, and CI runs `go test -race`, so concurrent calls are designed to be safe. A Decoder/Encoder wraps a single Reader/Writer and is not documented as shareable.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — toml.Unmarshal(data, &v) and toml.Marshal(v) have the same signatures as BurntSushi's, and both read the `toml` struct tag and fall back to case-insensitive field matching. But Decoder.Decode returns only an error (no MetaData), Decode(string)/DecodeFile/DecodeFS/Primitive do not exist, and Marshal output differs: single-quoted literal strings by default vs BurntSushi's double-quoted strings.

gotchas: All the dataset benchmarks (canada, twitter, citm_catalog, code, config, example) decode into interface{} and go through the dedicated fused path. EnableUnmarshalerInterface turns that path off, and struct targets use the reflect path, whose gain over the old v2 was smaller in PR #1067 (ReferenceFile/struct -45% time vs -67% for map).

Marshal writes strings as single-quoted literal strings unless they contain a newline or a single quote, and uses exact Go field names (e.g. `Version = 2`). Expect diffs in generated files after switching. The Marshal docs say nil interfaces and nil pointers are not supported, and uint64 values above MaxInt64 are rejected.
TOML local date-times decoded into time.Time are placed in time.Local. Use LocalDate/LocalTime/LocalDateTime to keep them unambiguous.

Open bug #1127: hex, octal and binary integers (0x10, 0o20, 0b10000) fail to decode into float64 fields, although they decode into interface{}. An independent GLD Serializer Benchmark run also reports spec-compliance misses for 2.4.3 (#1126, details only on its dashboard).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only Go entry among the TOML siblings: toml-spanner (Rust, vs the toml crate), teptris (C11, vs toml++) and TOMLDecoder (Swift Codable, vs toml++) are the picks in those languages. Choose go-toml v2 when the consumer is Go code that needs struct/map decoding through a familiar encoding/json-style API rather than an FFI parser.
verified_claims_summary: The README table comes from the project's own `go test -bench` harness (ci.sh benchmark -a: GOMAXPROCS=2, -count=10, benchstat sec/op ratios). The harness points the benchmark imports at go-toml v1 and at BurntSushi/toml, fetched with an unpinned `go get`. On the common cases, v2 beats BurntSushi by 2.4-2.6x on Marshal (5.0x for ReferenceFile/struct) and 5.9-6.4x on Unmarshal, with a 5.3x geomean over all 16 benchmarks. No Go version or CPU is stated for this table; PR #1067 separately measured old-v2 vs new-v2 on an Apple M1 Pro and a Threadripper PRO 3975WX with go1.26.4 (-53% and -56% geomean time).
status_note: Actively maintained, MIT-licensed side project (single maintainer per SECURITY.md). The latest tag is v2.4.3 (2026-07-05); the v2 branch is 7 commits ahead with unreleased bug fixes (last commit 2026-07-18), and only the latest 2.x receives security support.
